I am 55 years old and have been working these fields in Quzhou for 30 years. I know every inch of my 10.1 mu plot, and I know the rhythm of the North China Plain. With eight mouths in the household and some of my children sending money home from factory jobs in Handan, I have a little cushion, but I cannot afford to gamble everything. I need stable grain income and a cash crop on the side.

This spring, the winter wheat I sowed last October is greening up. That is my foundation. I will manage 7.6 mu as my wheat-maize double crop—the system that has never failed me—and I will put 2.5 mu into chili as a single spring crop. I do not intercrop them; I keep the chili on its own plot because it needs different watering and spraying schedules, and at my age I do not want the extra confusion.

For the wheat, I use an improved variety like Jimai 22. It is reliable. I will top-dress with urea at green-up and irrigate three times: green-up, jointing, and grain filling. I rotary till before sowing every autumn. I expect about 500 kg per mu if the weather holds. For pests, I will spray twice for insects and once for weeds or rust—that is what my neighbors do, and it works.

Come early June, as soon as the wheat is harvested, I will no-till sow hybrid maize—Denghai 605 or something similar from the county seed station. Summer is short; there is no time to plough. I will irrigate twice and spray three times total. Hybrid maize usually gives me about 550 kg per mu.

The 2.5 mu of chili is where I hope for cash. I will rotary till the beds, transplant hybrid seedlings in late April, and irrigate four times through the hot months. Chili is hungry for potassium and needs frequent spraying—about nine times in total, mixing insecticide and fungicide. It is labor-intensive, but with the family helping, we can manage. If the market price is decent, I expect around 2,600 kg of fresh chili per mu.

My well gives me water security, but pumping costs electricity, so I irrigate only when the crops truly need it. I buy my seeds and fertilizers from the agro-service center in town because I trust the county recommendations after all these years.
